The numerical model consists of 4094 shell elements with a characteristic length of 3 mm
Experimental tests used an impacting mass of 110 kg with an impact velocity of 8 m/s
The composite specimens tested had a height of 300 mm and nominal internal diameter of 70 mm
Numerical-experimental correlation showed 1.88% error in mean crash force and 0.12% error in absorbed energy
An initial trigger was created by selectively decreasing thickness by about one-fifth in the first two shell rings
The optimization domain includes major axis range of 60-110 mm, eccentricity range of 0.0-0.7, and taper ratio range of 0.5-1.0
A total of 90 finite element analyses were performed (30 sample points × 3 impact conditions)
Each FE analysis required more than 10 hours on a Pentium 4 1.5 GHz PC with 500 MB RAM
Maximum errors in RBF approximations ranged from 2.82% to 6.85% on verification points
The Pareto set identifies absorber shapes with the highest absorbed energy per unit mass
Optimal configurations achieved mass reduction up to 7% for vertical impacts
Optimal configurations achieved mass reduction of at least 20% for 20° angled impacts
The material used was Cytec Fiberite composite with 42% resin volume fraction
The stacking sequence consisted of four [0°/90°] oriented layers
The genetic algorithm used binary DNA codification with 24 bits total (8 bits per design variable)
Three distinct response surfaces were required to define each load-time curve (9 surfaces total)
Input and output data were normalized between 0 and 1 to improve RBF accuracy
The absorber height and stacking sequence were held constant during optimization
Conical shapes with moderate eccentricity provide better stability than cylindrical shapes
The major axis of the lower edge progressively increases along the Pareto curve
The taper ratio monotonically increases until reaching the maximum value of 1 along the Pareto curve
Load-shortening curves were approximated with bi-linear laws having equivalent absorbed energy
The optimization considered three different impact angles: 0°, 20°, and 30°
The framework uses spectral methods and partial differential equations for surface parameterization
